analysis.trend_summary: The Guatemala dataset shows a country with a stable, low-volatility macroeconomic profile and steady, diversified development-finance/private-sector investment activity, contrasted against very thin and largely ambiguous conflict/unrest signal. Conflict data (n=3, GDELT-sourced, CAMEO code 190/173) is low-severity-context and non-specific, offering little concrete evidence of organized political violence in the reporting window. Economic indicators (IMF/WorldBank, 2024-2026) point to moderate growth, low inflation, low government debt, and a positive current account -- a benign macro picture. Investment activity is dominated by energy PPPs and DFC financial-sector lending stretching back to 2014, indicating a long-running, sector-concentrated investment relationship rather than a recent surge. Humanitarian signals are almost entirely historical UNOSAT natural-hazard mapping (2017-2020 flooding, 2018 Volcán de Fuego eruption) rather than current crisis indicators.
analysis.security_analysis: The security picture cannot be substantively assessed from this data: only 3 conflict events are recorded, all from GDELT with CAMEO codes (190, 173) that denote unclear/unconventional actor interactions rather than confirmed armed violence, and two entries (2026-06-30, riotimesonline.com; 2026-06-30, reddeeradvocate.com) concern a historical-conflict-victims reburial ceremony in Chimaltenango and a U21 Pan Am sports event in Canada respectively -- neither indicates active conflict. No fatalities are recorded in any event. The absence of ACLED-sourced conflict data or corroborating detail means the "Security" dimension is effectively undetermined rather than low-risk.
analysis.political_stability_analysis: There is no clear protest, civil-unrest, or political-violence-targeting-civilians pattern in the supplied data. The one substantive conflict-adjacent item, the 2026-06-30 reburial of armed-conflict victims in Chimaltenango (Rio Times Online), references historical conflict legacy rather than an ongoing destabilization event, and a 2026-07-01 GDELT entry involving "AMBASSADOR <-> GUATEMALA" (CAMEO 161, cubaheadlines.com) is too vague to interpret as a stability signal. No strikes, riots, or civilian-targeting incidents are recorded in this window.
analysis.economic_analysis: IMF data show real GDP growth of 3.9% (2026 est.) and 4.1% (2025), consistent with WorldBank's 4.3% (2025) figure, alongside low inflation (IMF: 2.6% avg CPI 2026, 1.6% 2025; WorldBank CPI 1.5% in 2025) and very low reported unemployment (WorldBank: 2.6% in 2024-2025). Government debt is moderate and stable at 27.2-27.6% of GDP (IMF, 2025-2026), and the current account balance is positive (IMF: 3.2% of GDP 2026, 4.8% 2025; WorldBank: 2.9% in 2024), suggesting external-sector strength. External debt stock stood at $27.06B in 2024 (WorldBank) against net FDI inflows of only 1.6% of GDP the same year, indicating relatively modest foreign direct investment relative to the external debt base.
analysis.investment_analysis: Investment activity is dominated by two channels: the World Bank PPI private-sector database (49 of 61 investment records) and the U.S. DFC (12 records, plus 2 each from legacy OPIC/DCA). Energy generation is the largest identifiable sector, with a string of greenfield power projects from 2014-2024 -- Horus Energy ($100.0M, 2014), Escuintla Biomass ($74.2M, 2014), Horus Solar II ($60.0M, 2015), El Recreo II Hydro ($34.0M, 2015), Oxec Hydro Complex ($33.5M, 2014), Las Cumbres Wind Farm ($56.4M, 2019), and Yolanda Solar PV ($64.0M, 2024). DFC activity centers on finance-sector support -- Industrial DPR Funding Ltd. ($200.0M direct lending, FY2020; $150.0M, FY2018), Banco Promerica ($45.0M, FY2023), COSAMI R.L. ($20.0M, FY2024), and guarantees to Banco Internacional and BAC Guatemala (FY2018-2023) -- alongside smaller technical-assistance and political-risk-insurance instruments (DAI Guatemala, $2.0M, FY2022; Pomona IFII TAF, $750,000, FY2024). This pattern indicates sustained, diversified US and multilateral development-finance engagement concentrated in energy infrastructure and financial-sector intermediation rather than a single flagship project.
key_relationships: DFC has repeatedly financed the financial-intermediary sector in Guatemala, e.g. Banco Promerica S.A. ($45.0M, FY2023) and Industrial DPR Funding Ltd. ($200.0M, FY2020; $150.0M, FY2018), suggesting a recurring on-lending relationship for MSME/consumer credit.

World Bank PPI data shows a decade-long concentration of private greenfield energy projects (2014-2024), from Horus Energy ($100.0M, 2014) to Yolanda Solar PV ($64.0M, 2024), indicating continuity of private power-sector investment appetite.

A 2026-06-30 Rio Times Online item on reburial of armed-conflict victims in Chimaltenango points to unresolved historical-conflict legacy issues resurfacing in public discourse, though it is not indicative of current unrest.

UNOSAT humanitarian mapping clusters around 2017-2020 flooding events in Petén, Izabal, Alta Verapaz and Zacapa departments and the 2018 Volcán de Fuego eruption in San Miguel de Los Lotes, indicating recurring natural-hazard exposure in northern/central departments rather than conflict-driven humanitarian need.
risk_flags: Conflict data is extremely thin (n=3) and largely non-substantive (GDELT CAMEO 190/173 codes referencing sports and reburial events), making the Security dimension effectively unassessable from this dataset.
Net FDI inflows (1.6% of GDP, WorldBank 2024) are modest relative to the $27.06B external debt stock (WorldBank 2024), a ratio worth monitoring though not flagged as acute by the data itself.

Humanitarian signal is dominated by historical natural-hazard events (2017-2020 flooding, 2018 volcanic eruption) with no current-window humanitarian crisis indicators, so recent humanitarian conditions cannot be assessed.
analysis.data_caveats: This dataset contains no ACLED-sourced conflict records and only 3 low-specificity GDELT entries, so the security/conflict picture is not reliably characterized. Humanitarian/OSINT data is almost entirely historical (2017-2020), leaving a multi-year gap with no current humanitarian signal. Investment data, while numerous (n=61), is concentrated in only two source databases (World Bank PPI and DFC) and skews toward energy and finance sectors with project dates as far back as 2014, so it may not reflect the most recent investment climate.
